articles.text: Droves of Piedmont families gathered at Beach Elementary School last Sunday, September 7, to play, dance and draw at the 24th Annual Chalk Art Festival. The school’s blacktop was divided into 100 squares for kids to draw everything from dragons and aquatic animals to their favorite movie and video game characters. “It went great!” said event organizer Jon Schleuning. “We had great weather, great turnout as always. It was a lot of fun just seeing the blacktop explode into color.” Squares of “cement canvas” were available to purchase for $20, with all proceeds going to support art programs in Piedmont Schools. The event was aided by five student volunteers from the high school. Attending artists enjoyed music from DJ Criddy. “We sold pretty much all of our squares,” said Schleuning. “We had great involvement from kids and parents and families – we have people that come back every year, even after the kids have graduated from Beach.” Founded in 2002 by Havens art teachers Raul Jorcino and Karen Stanton, the event was moved to Beach School in 2008 Two kids collaborate on a chalk drawing at the 24th Annual Chalk Art Festival on the Beach School playground.

articles.text: Long-awaited pool project begins final testing period The Piedmont Community Pool project entered its final stage of completion last week as workers plastered the new competition and activity pools before filling them with water. The project now moves into the final system testing period known as commissioning. The pool’s project budget remains at $34.9 million, after being funded by $25.1 million in bonds and interest from measure UU which was approved by voters in November 2020. “Seeing water in the pools is extraordinary,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore. “With this milestone complete, our focus now shifts to commissioning – the critical, behind-thescenes work that prepares us for a safe and successful opening.” Commissioning is expected to last as long as six weeks while the pool equipment, filters, and heating are stress-tested. articles.text: Editor: I attended the Pancake Breakfast at Beach Elementary today. It was the 20th such celebration and my face is sore from so much smiling! The savory pancakes were highlights as always — that recipe could win a national competition! The appearance of the Fire Truck was also a treat, it’s amazing how many valves, knobs and capabilities those trucks have. But the thing that seemed new this year was a dunk tank where attendees could have extra fun by dunking people in a refreshing cold tub. I spat out a bite of my breakfast when the first person was dunked into the water. Piedmont has such a wonderful community feeling and events like the Pancake Breakfast reinforce how much community can matter. I would also like to propose that more events have dunk tanks, whether to celebrate, settle competitions or surprise guests! I can’t wait for the Wildwood Crab Feed and the Havens Game Night. I just hope if Wildwood has a dunk tank at their Crab Feed they don’t store the crabs in that dunk tank. –James Bohanion 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall Executive Editor: Misha Edel City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Tony Simons Evolette Mak, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: The Pardee Home Museum continues its Salon series on Sunday, September 14 at 4 p.m. with a presentation about poet Joaquin Oakland’s own Victorian poet was a walking, talking symbol of the Golden West. We remember him for his frontier ethics and bad boy antics but don’t fully understand his uplifting magnetism. Kristen Caven, the California Writers Club Writer in Residence at Joaquin Miller Park, will paint us a new picture of Joaquin Miller as America’s late romantic by introducing us to the many fascinating women who loved him. From the legendary Paquita, his Indian bride, to the “White Witch of Oakland,” his daughter Juanita, we’ll meet poets, actresses, heiresses, and the nation’s wealthKristen Caven is a creative dervish: as an author, playwright, cartoonist, lyricist, and independent historian, she is known as a dancer, poet and impresario, but her work is grounded in the field of mental health and wellness from a family perspective. Her unique perspectives on Oakland have given us fresh takes on Mills College (with her cartoon history, “Inside the Mills Revolution”), Oaktoberfest (with her animated play, “The Dirndl Diaspora” and her “Dirndl Diversity” fashion shows and movement), Lake Merritt (with her Pergola play, “Be Mused”), and her song, “Joaquin Miller Went Walkin’.” She’s also lectured to the Art Deco Societies of San Francisco and Miami Beach on the Virtures of Vintage Cookbooks. Her most recent book is The Uplift Family Playbook, an illustrated companion to The Winning Family: Where No One Has to Lose, and you can watch her last lecture, “Reconsidering Joaquin Miller” on the Oakland Public Library Youtube channel. articles.text: Piedmont High alum Kera Bartlett Binns is the lead organizer of Sun Day, a major clean energy event in Berkeley. The event will be held on Sunday, September 21 from 2:00–5:00 p,m, at the Willard Park Clubhouse, 2720 Hillegass Ave, Berkeley. RSVP to https://actionnetwork.org/events/sun-day-community-celebration-berkeley With many of the federal clean energy tax incentives sunsetting this year, now is a crucial time for Bay Area homeowners to learn how to electrify. This event demystifies the process in a fun, family-friendly way. It’s also a great fit for Piedmont residents looking for hands-on inspiration and access to local rebates and programs. The event includes: • Clean Energy Engagement Zone with expert clean energy guidance, demos of induction cooktops, portable solar panels, EV chargers, heat pumps, and more. • E-bike Try-It Zone on a closed section of Hillegass Avenue with test rides from Rad Power Bikes, Access Trikes, and Bay Wheels. • Speaker Panel featuring Rahul Young of Rewiring America, plus local homeowners, and non-profit leaders sharing reallife electrification stories • Kidical Mass Bike Ride, solar-powered s’mores, smoothie bikes, and hands-on kids’ activities • Food trucks and a community picnic Confirmed Engagement Zone Exhibitors (18+): Ava Community Energy City of Berkeley Office of Energy & Sustainable Development Sierra Club QuitCarbon Gradient Climate Health Now Acterra 350 Bay Area Ecology Center. For more information contact KeraBBinns@gmail.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles on Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. Excitement is revving up as nearly 100 vehicles have signed up to participate. Officer Tyler Petit, organizer of the car show, anticipates more than 120 unique cars to be on display this year. To accommodate the growing turnout, the event will expand from the Community Center parking lot down Magnolia Avenue to the base of Piedmont High School. This year’s show offers a chance for residents to meet the city’s new Police Chief, Frederick Shavies, along with members of the police department. The show promises to be a great opportunity to connect with local first Car Show organizer Officer Tyler Petit (left) with Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies. responders while enjoying a family friendly day surrounded by impressive cars and community spirit. Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, a local taco truck will be on site. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by retired Piedmont Police Sergeant Steve DeWarns in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and has had approximately 100 show worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. An aerial view of the car show from a drone

articles.text: A good Samaritan brought Dougie into the Oakland Animal Services shelter after he was found on the road having been hit by a car. Since having his severely broken back leg amputated, one-year-old Dougie has been recovering in a foster home and is getting better every day. Dougie is a sweet, social pup who loves to hang out with his foster family, but does just fine when left alone. He is house-trained and has been slowly but surely learning to navigate the world on three legs. He loves to snooze on his comfy dog bed (especially if it’s in the sun) and snuggle up with his humans so they can rub his chin. Dougie will need an adopter who can help him continue to build his confidence as he heals. articles.text: In my last article, I introduced the idea of Slow Made, a creative counter-movement to the AI fast lane. Much like the slow food revolution reminded us to savor the process of preparing and eating our meals, Slow Made is about reclaiming the joy and richness of the creative process. Sure, AI can whip up a “poem” or “paint” a picture in seconds. But if we shortcut the making, we miss out on the magic and the mess. We lose the process of wandering and discovering. The “I don’t know where this is going, but I’m going to let it unfold in front of me.” That’s the stuff creativity is made of. And that’s the part our brains actually need! And it’s not just for making art. It’s what we need for problem-solving, empathy, innovation, and connection. So the big question is: how do we keep the creative process alive and well in a world that wants everything done yesterday? Let’s talk about what Slow Made looks like in real life at work, at home, with kids, even on vacation. At Work: Think Before You Automate It’s tempting to let AI do the first draft of everything. Have an email to write? A proposal or report due? Even creative brainstorming for the next big idea can be outsourced these days. But what if, every once in a while, you started from scratch? Give yourself time to think. To sketch. To write something badly and then make it better. You’ll be surprised what ideas emerge when you allow for the imperfect. In fact, that’s where real innovation starts. It’s not in the perfect output, but in the messy in-between. Try this: Block 30 minutes of “blank page” time each week. Pick something you’d normally outsource to AI and don’t. Let your brain do the heavy lifting, even if it’s clunky at first. At Home: Create Before You Consume We all scroll. We all binge. But making something before you consume media can shift your whole day and your brain chemistry. Write a haiku on a sticky note and leave it for your spouse on the refrigerator door. Doodle while you make your breakfast. Play three chords on the piano in the corner. Try a new way to make sourdough. Make your brain produce before it absorbs. Try this: Start your morning with 10 minutes of making instead of 10 minutes of checking your phone. No rules. Just make. I keep a doodle journal and pens next to my bed so I can just make some fun shapes in interesting colors first thing in the morning. With Kids: Show the Process, Not Just the Product Kids are naturally Slow Made thinkers. They love the process. And then we start rushing them. (“Okay, great drawing, now let’s clean up!”) Instead, give them permission to follow their natural instincts. Sit down and draw with them. (Even if you think you “can’t draw”) Ask what happens next in their story. Let them see you creating too. Try this: Set up a “messy zone.” This could be a table or corner where creativity can happen without needing to be cleaned up right away. Celebrate the half-finished creation, the scribbled start of a story, the open-ended building project. Kids won’t finish most of what they start…that’s why they are creative geniuses! On Vacation: Make Time to Wander Vacations are prime territory for Slow Made thinking, but only if you stop scheduling every second. Give yourself unstructured time. Pack a sketchpad. Write in a travel journal. Capture moments in your own words, not just your camera roll. Wander a new city with no google maps. Sit and admire a sunset, watching all the way until the last speck of color is gone. Try this: Choose one creative ritual for your trip, for instance, journaling, sketching, photographing textures or doors or foliage…and do it daily. Not for Instagram, just for your own enjoyment. The Slow Made Mindset At its core, Slow Made isn’t about being anti-tech or going off the grid. It’s about being intentional. It’s about choosing to engage with the process and being open to whatever outcome does or does not manifest. When we create slowly, we reconnect with ourselves and each other. We open space for noticing and insight. So let’s give ourselves permission to go slow. Let’s make things. And those things might be terrible or beautiful or messy or all three. A creative life isn’t something you can rush. It’s something you make, one slow step at a time. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Speaker and Coach. https://ninameehan. com/

articles.text: More than 30 children’s authors will fill Children’s Fairyland with storytelling magic on Saturday, September 20 as the park celebrates books and 75 years of imagination. Fairyland’s Children’s Book Festival runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., welcoming more than 30 beloved and emerging children’s authors, illustrators, and storytellers from across the Bay Area. The festival brings together young readers, writers, and artists for a joyful day of storytelling, meet and greets, book signings, and interactive programming, all included with general admission. Throughout the park, families can meet authors and illustrators, hear stories read aloud by the creators themselves, watch illustration demos, and shop for books from the Books on B pop-up shop. “The Children’s Book Festival, originally known as Turn the Page, gives young readers a chance to meet the people behind the pages, discover new favorites, and feel the joy of being a part of a community that values literacy and the art of storytelling,” said Angela Moffett, Fairyland’s librarian. “For children who love books, and all lovers of children’s literature, the book festival at Fairyland is truly the best day of the year.” The festival also spotlights Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop, where young authors (ages 8–12) will share their original stories in an anthology, presenting alongside their mentor, local author, illustrator, and educator, Rob Liu-Trujillo. articles.text: Piedmont High School held its annual Club Day on Wednesday, Sept. 3, drawing hundreds of students eager to join campus organizations and connect with their peers. The event, coordinated by ASB leaders Grace Alonigreen and Dahlia Strub, featured more than 40 clubs, from established groups like Red Cross and Key Club to unique offerings such as Bio-Mart and the Food Blogging Club. Tables lined the breezeway as club leaders competed for attention with candy, hats, frisbees, and other giveaways. Identity-based organizations also played a prominent role this year. African Affinity Student Union, Advocacy for Asian Americans, GSA, and JSU all continued their missions of creating space for their respective communities. However, the Hispanic Student Union was notably absent. For many students, Club Day serves as both a launchpad for building community and a chance for leaders to help their organizations grow. The event’s popularity also brought challenges. Roughly a dozen clubs were not on the official lineup, some due to missing the registration deadline and others simply because of limited space, missing the chance to showcase their offerings to potential members. In particular, Flow Club, the group responsible for supplying menstrual products in the girls’ bathrooms, did not have a table. The absence of such groups raises broader questions about whether all student organizations are given equal opportunities to connect with their peers, and how those opportunities might extend beyond a single day. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School. Students check out a club during PHS Club Day.

articles.text: Staff Photos Edie Elmquist runs into the end zone for a touchdown against Miramonte Piedmont High’s flag football team claimed its first win of the season on Thursday, September 4 at Witter Field, beating the Miramonte Matadors in a defensive battle, 12-6. Piedmont scored the game’s opening touchdown thanks to a fumbled snap by Miramonte deep on their side of the field. On a punt attempt, the Matadors’ center snapped the ball over the punter’s head, leading to a dead ball at the four yard line. It led to quarterback Edie Elmquist finding Stephanie Lee for a touchdown moments later. “It’s rare for us to go up first, so I think we felt the mental energy from that. Miramonte made some adjustments, and our players responded with their own adjustments,” said PHS coach Beth Black. The Highlanders increased their lead to 12-0 with 2:34 left in the second quarter on a two-yard carry by Elmquist. The sophomore quarterback has proven to be the leader of Piedmont’s offense, using her speed to break the pocket, and an arsenal of moves to make flag-pullers miss. Now in her second year as the team’s quarterback, Elmquist is showing a deeper knowledge of the game, poise, and quick thinking to make plays. She credits her rapid development to playing club flag football. “At the end of last season, I just thought, ‘I need more.’ So all summer and softball season I worked to get better. I was running, I was lifting, and played with another team. That gave me a lot of confidence,” Elmquist said. Senior safety Dahlia Osman had two interceptions, one in the first quarter and another in the third. She has recorded a pair of interceptions in all three games this season. Osman moved to safety during her junior season in 2024 after playing at cornerback as a sophomore. Using her speed and flag pulling ability, Osman is in the perfect spot, roving the field as the defense’s playmaker. “I like playing back there and being an interrupter,” Osman said. “Last year, I was switched into playing safety during the season after starting out at corner. This year, I’ve become much more comfortable back there and I know what to watch for.” Game Recap Both teams traded possession in the first quarter, leading to Miramonte’s botched punt attempt. Taking over at the four, Piedmont scored on second down when Elmquist found Lee for the touchdown with 2:03 left. Elspeth Grippando (left) celebrates after recording an interception. Dahlia Osman recorded two interceptions against Miramonte, giving her six this season.

Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team appears to be turning the corner after sweeping Hayward 3-0 at the Farmers’ gym on Thursday, September 4 by scores of 25-18, 25-14, and 25-18. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 4-3 through seven matches, which eclipses last year’s season total of 3-19. “We’re such a young team, but we’re going to give our league a run for their money,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “Today wasn’t the best display, but there’s something about us that gives us a spark. We can see potential at the end of the tunnel,” If all goes well for the Highlanders, they are likely to finish this season with a winning record and possibly their first North Coast Section berth since 2018. “There are seven sophomores to fill important roles. We have the skill and have more wins than last year,” Cardenas said. Maika Ting, one of eight new players, recorded eight kills against Hayward. “It’s been really amazing to be a part of this team. We have a bunch of sophomores who I know really well. Everyone and is really encouraging,” Ting said. Against the Farmers, the home side was able to keep things close in each set until Piedmont powered home the win. Piedmont clung to a narrow 15-13 advantage before limiting Hayward to just one point to finish the second set. In the third there were eight lead changes until the Highlanders went ahead for good at 17-16. Maiki Ting, a sophomore, had eight kills against Hayward. In the second set, both teams traded points back and forth for the better half of the set. With Piedmont holding to a 15-13 lead, they added three straight points before Hayward’ next point to hold an 18-14 advantage. pages.text: Wednesday, September 10, 2025 15 HIKING WITH JON Hiking with elephants through a Thailand sanctuary By Jonathan Comeaux [From August 2023] When visiting Chiang Mai and the northern province of Thailand, it’s clear to see the region’s cultural ties to elephants with countless merchants having trinkets, clothing, and jewelry of elephants on display. If you’re visiting Chiang Mai, travelers are bound to run into offices for sanctuaries looking to lure in tourists, so it is important to do your research to ensure you’re investing your experience with the right company which treats its elephants ethically. With that, the Post visited Into The Wild The Post visited an elephant sanctuary on the outskirts of Chiang Mai, Thailand. Elephants coating themselves with dirt to cool off while on the trail. Walking through a thick jungle in Doi Inthanon National Park Elephant Camp on the outskirts of Chiang Mai. In Thailand, elephants are tied to the nation’s history in religion and royalty. They are considered guardians of Buddha, Earth and Thailand’s temples. They were also used in ancient wars to defend the country, while ownership of them was considered a sign of status. However, the species has decreased from the 300,000 wild elephants during the 20th century to an estimated 3,084-3,500 now with an estimated 4,000 in captivity. When choosing an elephant sanctuary to visit, it’s important to decide against places that host rides, keep their elephants in enclosed areas, and has a proper diet for the elephants—all of which is considered animal cruelty. Elephants, which have a typical lifespan of 60-70 years, can have a severe drop in life expectancy when kept in improper conditions, with some cases as high as a 50 percent drop. Into The Wild Elephant Camp have seven elephants in a large encampment about 40 miles outStaff Photos An elephant searching to see if the Post’s journalist had any treats. side of Chiang Mai in the Doi Inthanon National Park. Their elephants are in an open space alongside the Mae Tian River, allowing you to learn about the species, its history, and natural habitat. As the guides at Into The Wild explained, it is difficult to release domesticated elephants back into the wild given they are intelligent creatures with good memories, meaning they will seek out humans in order to get food. Into The Wild specializes in finding other domesticated elephants that may have not had ideal living conditions in its previous home. “Elephants have been living with people for many generations, so they generally rely on people. It’s really difficult for them to return to the wild by themselves. They have a really big brain, so when they are used to being fed by people, it’s hard for them to find their own food because they know humans will feed them,” explained Mike, a guide at Into The Wild. After feeding the elephants, they offered a brief hike through the jungle alongside the elephants, observing how they naturally live in the wild—finding dirt pits to throw on themselves and trees to topple over as they scratch their backsides. Guides also point out edible foliage for foraging and how local tribes have used different species of plants for uses like medicine, insect repellent, and cuisine. The hike puts you in close quarters with the Thailand wilderness. articles.text: Black Gold: Stories Untold, a major art exhibition highlighting the transformative impact of Black communities on California’s cultural, social, and political worlds, is now on view at Fort Point National Historic Site in the Presidio. Black Gold features artwork by 17 contemporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War, including never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred HowBrian Kemble, curator of Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek Ruth Bancroft Gardens is honoring its longtime curator and horticulturist Brian Kemble on Thursday, September 25. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees thousands of cacti and succulent species that grow on the garden’s three acres. As curator, he is in charge of hybridizing plants or finding two plants that have complementary characteristics and combining them to create new species. Kemble worked closely with Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, who was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public. Kemble will be in conversation with Dick Turner, the garden’s first Executive Director, and will share stories of working alongside the Bancroft, how he’s seen the garden transform over the decades and his reflection on what he wants his enduring legacy to be. Guests are invited to stay for a reception with beverages and light fare following the presentation and conversation. Ticket holders may join in to raise a glass to Kemble’s legacy and work. All ticket sales help fund Kemble’s “Bed 12” project, the first flower bed Ruth worked on in the garden. Donations and ticket proceeds benefit the restoration and revitalization of Bed 12. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco unveils Unbound: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, a group exhibition exploring connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies, on October 1. The new exhibition, organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. Unvound includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past 20 years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND A new exhibition at MoAD was organized by Key Jo Lee, Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs. will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org.

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony will perform a free community concert at the Great Meadow in Golden Gate Park on Sunday, September 21, concluding the 10th annual Flower Piano festival. The unique event merges botanical beauty and classical music against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the San Francisco Botanical Garden, places grand pianos and throughout the gardens where musicians and artists will perform. The festival concludes on Sunday, September 21 with performances by San Francisco Symphony musicians in Golden Gate Park’s Great Meadow from 12 p.m. to 1 p.m. The concert is free for San Francisco residents who present a valid driver’s license. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Big Hero 6 Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of kids and family. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Fransokyo, where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro, who graduated from high school at the age of 14, spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s night-time antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. They hope to influence the young prodigy to give up his underground exploits, and come to the realization that there is a world beyond his own niche of homegrown high tech stuff. As it turns out, the visit to the university proves a success. Hiro, captivated, meets kindred spirits, sees advanced labs, and meets the distinguished Professor Callaghan (James Cromwell), head of robotics, and the inventor of a medical bot, Baymax (Scott Adsit), programed to care for his charge. It eventually becomes Hiro’s sidekick of sorts. Of course, there is a sudden turn of events, which impacts Hiro and his buds, and they soon discover that as a result, their lives have been turned upside down. What occurs? Well, they unexpectedly discover an ominous, dangerous plot that pulls the gang into a harrowing adventure that is brimming with fun, action, and imaginative science (an example being a swarm of buzzing microbots). Older kids, tweens and teens will find Big Hero 6 a compelling watch, and Hiro an interesting role model. The world of high tech/A.I. is upon us. Hiro is already there. Big Hero 6. articles.text: Joan Moffitt Drum, a lifelong Bay Area resident, passed away on July 29, 2025 in Alameda after a long illness. She was the daughter of Albert H. Moffitt Jr. and Barbara Seale Moffitt of Alameda. Born in Oakland in 1938, Joan was raised in Alameda, where she attended Franklin and Haight elementary schools. The competition pool was full by the morning of Thursday, September 4. Next up was the activity pool on Friday, September 5. Crews started plastering the bed of the pool in the early morning. Since the second pool was smaller, it was filled completely within the day. A time-lapse video of the filling process is available on the City of Piedmont Youtube page at https://youtu.be/wcntHMLBri4. Filling the pools with water marks a major milestone and allows the project to begin the commissioning phase – beginning with the filters, then moving on to the chemical and control systems. While commissioning is underway, the pool water may start to look cloudy or “milky” for a few days. This is an expected part of the process, as the systems are stress-tested beyond everyday use to ensure that there are no issues.
